chapter: Pranks, the Mingus fight and Duke's writing
title: Mercer Ellington's book on brass versus reeds
summary: Willard quotes Mercer that Duke loved loud trombones and later lavished attention on saxophones; Tizol disagrees and doesn't recall saying it.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Who?
Mercer Ellington's book; this book, 'Duke Ellington In Person', the one that Mercer wrote.
Mercer's book?
Uh huh.
Oh, you mean, that little magazine or something?
Oh, you read the Jet article about that.
Yeah.
Yeah. I see. So But you haven't read the whole book.
No.

Because he makes several references to you in the book. In Mercer's book, 'Duke Ellington in Person', by Mercer Ellington and Stanley Dance, Danna, they say, || In reference to Duke's composing, about his search for color and a technique that was more or less related to the art of painting. I don't know how much this matter of color related to dynamics, although Juan Tizol, who played valve trombone in the orchestra, always told me, 'Your papa likes to hear the

trombones play loud, and the trombones were always Pop's favorite section in the band. At one point, he was more interested in brass than anything else, and then quite suddenly, he seemed to become much more intrigued by the potential of the reed section.

"In later years, when I was in the band, most of the time, at a record date or a rehearsal, was spent going over the saxophone parts. I used to get quite peeved, because every once in awhile, the brass section had things to play that we knew we could do better; it was a matter of running over them two or three times before finally making a take -- but there would be only a brief run through for the brass at the session, while the greatest attention was lavished on the saxaphones.
"Yet, all through the years, he was searching for tones of color, as you can hear in creations like 'Mood Indigo' and 'Azure.'"
What do you think about that? I mean, do you agree with Mercer?
I don't quite understand all that.

Well, he says that Duke, that you told him that Duke always wanted the trombones to play loud, and, at one point, Duke liked the brass and concentrated more on brass writing than on reeds, and then later, he said, according to Mercer, he was very, very interested in the
reed section, and almost ignored the brass section. Do you think that's right?

I don't know; maybe when Mercer was himself in the brass section -- but when we had a good brass section, I never heard him squawking about the brass section or anything like that, and paid attention to the reed section.
Uh huh. Did you tell Mercer that his father always wanted the trombones to play loud? Do you think ..
No, I don't know anything about that.
